item.title: Trump says Zelensky 'doesn't want to end this war' after Ukraine hits Russian terminal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ukraine launched one of its biggest drone attacks this year on Russia overnight on Saturday, hitting a key oil terminal in defiance of US President Donald Trump’s demand it stop hitting Russian energy infrastructure. There have been growing tensions between Ukraine and the US in recent days, prompting fears in Kyiv it could lose essential support as it approaches another winter under relentless Russian attack. Trump on Friday invoked a waiver exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress. President Volodymyr Zelensky later told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the US siding with Russia would be a “historic mistake.” Smoke rises above the city following an air attack on the oil terminal in Saint Petersburg, Russia, on October 18, 2026 - AFP/Getty Images Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday that he doesn’t want to do anything that will drive Russia away from negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, adding that he believes “great progress is being made.” At the same time, he excoriated Zelensky, saying that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.” “I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote. Despite this, the Ukrainian president said he spoke to US envoy, Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Sunday as part of “nonstop communication” to work towards to goal of peace. “We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer,” Zelensky posted on X . But Ukraine is keeping up long-range strikes into Russia. Russia’s defense ministry said it shot down 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight into Sunday over various parts of the country. One target was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, according to Russian authorities. The terminal can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year. Ukraine’s Fire Point company, which makes the drones used in the attack, said there was a fire on the terminal’s grounds following the strike. A logistics centers in St. Petersburg was also attacked, according to Ozon, a Russian distribution company, as well as a data center for the Russian VKontakte social media platform. One person was killed and five wounded in the attacks, with residential homes damaged as well, according to local authorities. “They shot one down right above us: there was one bright flash, and it shook us up quite strongly,” a 41-year old resident of St. Petersburg told CNN. “I heard a roar, got everyone out of their beds, took the cat, and we hid in the bathroom,” another said. A deepening spat Ukraine’s strikes come amid Zelensky’s deteriorating relationship with Trump, who last week called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace.” A week ago, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure, as the White House tries to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices ahead of crucial midterm elections. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such an agreement. Ukraine briefly halted such attacks, but has since resumed them — while Russia never stopped pounding Ukraine’s energy plants and cities. Eleven people were killed and nearly 50 injured across Ukraine in Russian missile and drone attacks in the 24 hours to Sunday morning, according to Ukrainian authorities, including what they called a massive attack on energy facilities in the Odesa region. “Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ​ago, Russia has ​deliberately ‌attacked ​Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors ⁠76 times,” Zelensky ​wrote on X Sunday. People watch the burning oil terminal following an air attack in Saint Petersburg, Russia, on October 18, 2026. - AFP/Getty Images Trump has waived sanctions on imports of Russian diesel and on Friday invoked a waiver exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress, sparking criticism even from Republicans . In an interview Sunday with “Meet the Press,” Zelensky said the waiver strengthened Putin’s war against Ukraine while Moscow was failing on the battlefield. He said it was “more support for Russian aggression.” Zelensky also repeated that the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink system to guide its short-range and battlefield drones was still curtailed. “It was a message from the American government” to limit the speed at which Ukrainian drones could fly, Zelensky said. The Trump administration has denied it ordered the service restricted. Zelensky said that intelligence sharing had been blocked by the US side for three days during ballistic missile attacks but had since been restored. US satellite networks have been critical in providing the Ukrainian military with warnings of incoming missiles. A Ukrainian source told CNN there was no early warning before a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on Sunday. This is the third time in a week there has not been an early warning. Zelensky was also asked about Trump’s comments that he was more difficult to deal with than Russian President Vladimir Putin and replied it was “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.” Zelensky said he wanted to trust Trump and hoped he would change his attitude to Putin. Asked if Trump was an ally of Ukraine, Zelensky said: “I hope so.” Daria Tarasova, Julia Benbrook and Jennifer Hanlser contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/18/europe/ukraine-russia-drone-attack-trump-intl

item.title: Obama condemns comments by 'border czar' that Ilhan Omar could be denaturalized
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Homeland security officers carry boxes from the Washington DC residence of Ilhan Omar, on 12 October. Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/AP Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her. Obama wrote Sunday morning, on X , that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.” He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs, adding: “if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her – or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.” Obama, too, has had his citizenship scrutinized by Trump, who more than a decade ago fueled false conspiracy theories that Obama was born in Kenya and therefore not eligible to be president. Related: Ilhan Omar’s attorneys say federal search of her home was ‘neither justified nor lawful’ Tom Homan , Trump’s “border czar”, was asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”. “If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before. “And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.” Homan’s comments were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a top Trump administration official since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October. The search of Omar’s home sparked major backlash and accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized about denaturalizing and deporting . The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the November midterm elections , in which Omar is on the ballot. Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details. “I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.” Omar – a naturalized US citizen from Somalia – was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020. Obama stated in his post on X that Omar arrived in the US with her father when she was 12, and five years later, when her father became a naturalized citizen, she became one, too, because she was 17. (An 18-year-old would have had to apply for citizenship separately, he noted.) “Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” he wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone – all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.” In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneys accused the US justice department of potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy. The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its on offensive on legal migration . The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship. As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings. Nonetheless, as of April, the US justice department had reportedly identified nearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate. The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also include allegations that her ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US. Related: Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says The federal government reportedly seized Omar’s phone during the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives. Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search. Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers. There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal . Even veterans at the Department of Justice expressed shock over the targeting of Omar, according to reporting by NBC News . “I was astounded to see a search of a sitting congressperson this close to an election,” said Peter Carr, a former career justice department spokesperson, NBC News reported. “Historically, the department has been very adamant that politics plays no role in investigative decisions they make and they try very hard to avoid taking overt actions that might even have the perception of influencing an election.” After the raid on her home, Omar posted on X that she was “ok”. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” “I will not be silenced,” Omar added. This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/trump-border-czar-says-ilhan-171602251.html

item.title: Trump endorses Netanyahu just 9 days before Israeli elections
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The relationship between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin and US President Donald Trump, shown in April, 2025, has soured ahead of crucial elections. - Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images/FILE With just over a week to go until Israel’s election day, President Donald Trump finally gave the full-throated endorsement that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had long sought. The president called Netanyahu a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” in a post on social media, which he said serves as his “Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu.” Trump also hinted at a possible resumption of hostilities in the unpopular war with Iran — a war the US launched alongside Israel eight months ago — saying that if the Iranians do not “change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job.” Netanyahu was quick to respond, thanking Trump for the “tremendous support and the joint work.” Trump told Axios journalist and CNN Global Affairs analyst Barak Ravid in a brief phone interview that he had always intended to endorse Netanyahu. “I was always going to do that. I just didn’t want to do it too soon,” he said. Trump added that they have a “good relationship” and would “continue to do well” together if Netanyahu is reelected, according to Ravid. “It is important that Israel has a person they can count on,” Trump said. It was an endorsement that seemed uncertain until it finally arrived and cannot mask what has become at times a rocky relationship between the two. For years, Israelis driving the country’s highways in the final weeks of an election have seen the same image: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu standing beside President Donald Trump, under the slogan, “A different league.” Less than two weeks before the October 27 vote, the billboards of Netanyahu are back. But this time Trump is not on them. The president still appears in some videos for Netanyahu’s Likud party, but his absence may signal something beyond advertising. Until Sunday, Trump had held off endorsing Netanyahu. “I’m not involved in [Israeli] politics anymore,” he told Time earlier this month. On Thursday, Trump told Newsmax that Netanyahu would like him to be involved in the election. “I’ve had a very good relationship with him,” he said, but avoided endorsing him again. When asked directly whether he trusts Netanyahu, he said bluntly, “I don’t trust anybody in the world of politics.” Trump has starred in Netanyahu’s campaigns since 2013, when still a businessman and TV personality, he released a video urging Israelis to “vote for Benjamin.” When Trump entered the White House in 2017, he showered Netanyahu with political gifts. About two weeks before Israel’s April 2019 election, Netanyahu was in Washington to watch Trump sign a historic proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights. In January 2020, five weeks before Israelis went again to the polls, Trump unveiled the Israeli-Palestinian “Deal of the Century” plan. Netanyahu stood smiling by his side. Ahead of this election, there has been no red carpet. The last time Netanyahu and Trump met at the White House in August, there were no cameras. The two did not meet at all when Netanyahu traveled to New York for the UN General Assembly in September. Demonstrators protest against Netanyahu's address to the UN General Assembly in New York in September. His efforts to undercut peace talks have drawn bipartisan ire. - David Dee Delgado/Reuters A protesters against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies is arrested after blocking a street next to the United Nations. - Spencer Platt/Getty Images Over the course of the last year, Netanyahu has taken steps that have drawn fury from Trump, including undermining Trump-led peace efforts by striking inside Lebanon and Gaza. Trump has cursed the prime minister out in phone calls and warned him he’s losing support among Americans, according to people familiar with the conversations. He’s asked why Israel was blowing up apartment buildings in Lebanon and warned about the risk of a global economic downturn as a result of the Iran war. Inside the White House, many of the moves were interpreted as election-year posturing by Netanyahu, whose internal politics are well known by Trump and his advisers. Over the summer, many Trump advisers came to the conclusion that Netanyahu was trying to prolong the Iran war to bolster his own political standing. Trump has given Netanyahu a degree of leeway because of those political concerns, people familiar with the matter said. But he’s still grown frustrated at some of Israel’s actions, many of which he believes run counter to American interests. Another person close to Trump suggested his lack of endorsement had been tied to Netanyahu’s weakness in the polls. Trump has long been careful to avoid endorsing candidates who seem likely to lose. In conversations over the past several months, Trump has quizzed Netanyahu about the election and his prospects, according to people familiar with the matter. While Netanyahu has sought to project confidence, Trump is well aware of the prime minister’s difficult political position. As Netanyahu’s standing fell in the Trump administration, so did Trump’s standing in Israel. According to Israeli sources close to Netanyahu, Trump was originally meant to be a centerpiece of Netanyahu’s campaign. Last December, at Mar-a-Lago, the prime minister announced that Trump would become the first non-Israeli to receive the prestigious Israel Prize. Netanyahu aides hoped Trump would accept the prize in person at Israel’s Independence Day ceremony in April, giving jumpstarting the campaign. Then came the war with Iran. A smoke plume rises following a missile strike on a building in Tehran on March 1, 2026. - Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images The joint US-Israeli attack began on February 28 with the two leaders projecting strategic harmony. Netanyahu thanked “my friend, President Donald Trump,” calling him “a leader who stands by his word.” Trump described the two of them as “war heroes” and publicly demanded that Israel’s president grant Netanyahu a pardon in his ongoing corruption trials. But Trump never showed interest in attending the Israel Prize ceremony. By then, the fighting in Iran had ended and ceasefire talks were underway. The Iran ceasefire and subsequent memorandum of understanding were deeply unpopular in Israel, particularly on the right. Yinon Magal, a pro-Netanyahu TV anchor, called Trump a “loser” after the deal was signed. A July survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute found that only 7% of Israelis had “a great deal of trust” that Trump “will do the right thing” on US-Israel relations, and 45% had none. “Trump’s stock in Israel, especially among right wing-voters, has weakened,” a Likud source said. “An endorsement would not necessarily have helped Netanyahu so much, so he did not invest much in it.” Another Likud source said, “It’s not as if Trump will endorse any other opponent, so it’s nice to have, but not a must.” US President Donald Trump leaves the stage after speaking during a campaign rally at the Freeman Coliseum on October 07, in San Antonio, Texas. - Win McNamee/Getty Images Netanyahu’s opponents are watching, but with less alarm than before. “A year ago, our camp was calling anyone close to Trump to prevent an endorsement,” one senior opposition figure said ahead of Sunday’s news. “Now it doesn’t really matter, the charm is not there.” When Trump was asked specifically about who is currently polling as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, he said, “Well, I don’t know, I don’t hear bad things about him.” He then said, “They’ve written Bibi off many, many times, just like they’ve written me off many, many times. I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.” Trump has his own reasons for distance. American public opinion of Israel has fallen sharply, declining even more against the backdrop of the Iran war. Israel’s average net favorability fell from +51 points in July 2018 to -16 in July 2026, according to multiple polls, a 67-point drop over eight years. As America quickly soured on the Iran war, a source familiar with the relationship said, Trump has been “trying to shed the image that Netanyahu pulled him into it.” Still, the apparent distance may be misleading. Israeli sources say the two leaders have recently discussed renewed strikes on Iran. Israeli security sources told CNN preparations are underway - pending Trump’s decision - with timing unclear because of the US midterm elections. Netanyahu rejected suggestions he was seeking escalation before the vote. “It is not convenient for us, it’s no good,” he told Army Radio this week. He complained that if Iran fired missiles at Israel, his opponents “will blame me.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/18/world/trump-netanyahu-elections-relations-intl

item.title: What are self-replicating 'AI worms', and why is Anthropic worried about them?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
‘Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.’ Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/Reuters Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about. Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each. Related: AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devices In addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort. “It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort. “I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be.” The damage of such “AI worms” could be astonishingly large. Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet. That legacy includes the Morris worm of 1988, which arrived before the mainstream consumer internet, when a graduate student released a program that took advantage of various software flaws and weak passwords, copying itself so rapidly that many infected machines slowed to a stop. The US and Israel brought worms into international espionage with the stealthy Stuxnet in the lat 2000s, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges. Other worms like the Russian NotPetya and North Korean-attributed WannaCry have caused tens of billions of dollars’ worth of damage worldwide. Many of the world’s most destructive worms have depended on known vulnerabilities that device owners have not patched, sometimes months after patches became available. The Anthropic team predicted that a worm like theirs could function in the same way and be harder to stop, because smart devices receive patches less often than phones or laptops. Worse, they theorized that an AI worm could keep adapting to other types of hardware by researching newly disclosed vulnerabilities. What differentiates AI worms from typical reproducing viruses is that AI models can learn as they go, said Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early security expert at OpenAI who now runs AI security startup RunSybil. Existing cybersecurity infrastructure is not ready for the proliferation of such threats, Herbert-Voss said. “We need to better enable our security teams. We need to be giving them more resources to fix problems.” Worms could also be used for benevolent purposes, suggested Chris Inglis, a former deputy director of the National Security Agency who served as National Cyber Director in the Biden White House. “The question of whether AI worms are plausible has been settled by several breakout events over the past six months,” Inglis said by digital message. “The better question is how we will employ them, counter them, and/or combine them with other emerging technologies.” Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end. Their research follows a paper published by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm. “The capabilities have been developing very rapidly,” said co-author and Toronto PhD student Jonas Guan. Guan and other experts said that, as a practical matter, an AI worm should not top anyone’s list of AI fears. The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers. Basic security hygiene, including requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication, would stop most worms and other hacking, experts said. “Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, vice-president of research at security firm SentinelOne. “It’s nifty stunt hacking that’s getting way more amplification in service of the ridiculous doomer narratives that suggest models have a mind and will of their own.” Anthropic did not respond to an interview request. Outside Washington, many in the AI and security worlds believe greater government oversight of AI is now essential. But members of Congress have introduced mutually conflicting bills, while the White House has so far created only a small review board . Security researchers and laypeople alike find themselves weighing the motivations behind fearful prognostications from AI companies, which range from espousing quasi-religious beliefs, to seeking legislation to exclude rivals or save money, to hyping the anticipated multi-trillion-dollar public valuations of the San Francisco AI giants. “The claim that a lot of this is marketing is correct, but the reality dwarfs any PR,” said Gadi Evron, who is running a conference on AI security in San Francisco this month called Unprompted. “Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.” This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://tech.yahoo.com/cybersecurity/articles/self-replicating-ai-worms-why-133000706.html

item.title: Rubio says Trump will take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Nandita Bose and Gram Slattery Oct 17 (Reuters) - The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, ‌while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation. Rubio said on Saturday that ‌the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier. "A lot of you don't ​know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham ‌Act, which he signed last month at ⁠the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine. The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next ⁠week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review. "I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and ​even to ​the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip ​to Uzbekistan. Friday's executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, ‌who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war. DIESEL SUPPLIES Rubio on Saturday also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies. "That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get." Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of ‌diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond. The ​diesel agreement is "a carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline" ​to Russia, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said ​during a Sunday interview on ABC's "This Week." But "the only way they can get additional diesel to export is ‌if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine," Wright told ​CNN's "State of the Union" program ​on Sunday. “If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” he told CNN. “He's putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.” Rubio said ​the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected ‌the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies. "These conflicts around ​the world are starting to crash into each other," he said. (Reporting by Nandita Bose in Kentucky, Gram Slattery in ​Washington and Doyinsola Oladipo; Editing by Sergio Non and Christopher Cushing) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/rubio-says-trump-60-days-033841652.html

item.title: U.S. taking Putin's side would be a 'historic mistake,' says Zelensky
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S.’ formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake” but said he still sees President Donald Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill. “We want to trust him,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday, referring to Trump. “I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help United States.” Trump on Friday waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, saying in an executive order that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.” Passed with bipartisan support and signed by Trump last month , the sanctions were intended to target Russia’s revenue streams by punishing global buyers of Russian oil and gas. Trump defended his decision Sunday, writing on Truth Social that he did not want to “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” Trump added that Zelenskyy was targeting diesel refineries in Russia, which he claimed was “seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.” Trump added that “Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way,” a claim that comes the same day the Russian Foreign Affairs Ministry announced that Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov would travel to Tehran this week. The waiver came days after a deal with Putin to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar was announced. At the same time, Zelenskyy said, U.S. intelligence sharing was briefly “blocked,” blinding Ukraine to incoming ballistic missiles, while limits have been placed on Starlink technology critical to intercept jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy told moderator Kristen Welker that Ukrainian officials believe the decision to limit Starlink, imposed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, came in response to a “message from American government.” The U.S. has been Ukraine’s most significant backer across 4½ years of war, but personal relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have appeared severely strained in recent weeks, with each publicly criticizing the other. Asked about Trump’s remark last week that he was “more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Zelenskyy said he was “very honest” with Trump. “Maybe it’s not very polite,” he said, but it is “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.” Zelenskyy, who accused the U.S. of betraying Kyiv last week, said his feelings have not changed. He warned that Trump’s diesel deal with Russia “will strengthen Putin in his will to occupy us.” Announcing the deal last week, Trump expressed hopes that it would go some way to address soaring fuel costs. But Zelenskyy said the deal wouldn’t have “a real influence” on the price of oil in the U.S. because the rising prices were due to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine. “I don’t know all the reasons why President Trump makes such deals,” he said. Of the prospect of the U.S.’ more formally siding with Russia, he said: “If these two countries will be together ... we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand.” Zelenskyy said it was a “pity” Trump had waived the sanctions in a bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who he said was “a great supporter of peace and of Ukraine.” “He invested his life and time because he really believed in Ukraine,” he said. In a separate interview on “Meet the Press,” Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., defended Trump’s decision to lift the Russia sanctions. “He’s trying to walk this fine balance between trying to be able to put pressure on Russia, but also to be able to help the American people, so he is choosing the American people first is what he’s doing,” Lankford said, pointing to high gas prices. Asked whether Trump’s moves indicate the president is siding with Putin, Lankford, a member of the Intelligence Committee, said Trump was “siding with the free people of Ukraine,” adding later that Trump was working to get the two countries “to the table to be able to negotiate.” The war has seen little recent movement on the front line, with Russia continuing to occupy around a fifth of Ukraine. Trump had vowed to end the conflict within days of the start of his second term, but peace talks have effectively stalled, with Ukraine saying that Russia has rejected a short-term ceasefire and that Putin’s terms for peace are tantamount to a full surrender. Meanwhile, another difficult winter looms for Ukrainian civilians, with a critical munitions shortage limiting Zelenskyy’s ability to defend infrastructure against Russian strikes. Zelenskyy said he was due to speak to U.S. negotiators by phone later Sunday and was still hopeful of a meeting in the days ahead. “I’m very open for this, even with all the difficult circumstances,” he said. He cited some progress after a multiday interruption in U.S. intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which he said has now been “deblocked.” “We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.” European and Ukrainian officials previously told NBC News they believed that a move to limit sharing intelligence , coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia, was most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv to make concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks. While Zelenskyy indicated that the intelligence problem has been resolved, he said Ukraine was still facing an ongoing speed restriction on its use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink service. Asked whether he thought Trump or Musk had directly made the decision to limit Starlink, Zelenskyy said he did not know but thought “both” were involved. He said that if Trump decided tomorrow to lift the restriction, “it will immediately work as it was before.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. item.title: Trump's most controversial moves have something in common: This DOJ office
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When White House officials wanted to know if President Donald Trump could send the U.S. military to help capture President Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a special unit in the Justice Department assured them it was legal. When the administration was preparing to strike suspected drug traffickers’ boats on the open sea without congressional approval, the same small unit declared the action permissible. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. When the White House asked if the Presidential Records Act was constitutional, the office ruled it was not, giving Trump the apparent green light to save fewer records from his second term. As the Trump administration pushes the bounds of executive power, the Justice Department unit known as the Office of Legal Counsel, or OLC, has affirmed some of its most high-profile and controversial actions - even as many experts question their legitimacy and some are later struck down by the courts. Tucked away on the Justice Department’s fifth floor, the two dozen or so lawyers at the OLC are charged with assessing the legality of actions the executive branch wants to take, especially those that are novel or likely to be contentious. Much of its work, particularly on national security matters, remains shielded from public view, but some of the office’s conclusions have emerged in often dense legal opinions. The OLC during Trump’s second term is not the first to be accused of adopting shaky reasoning to justify a president’s policies. Under President Barack Obama, the OLC wrote a controversial rationale for launching a deadly drone attack on a U.S. citizen overseas. Under President George W. Bush, the office justified the used of “enhanced interrogation” - what some call torture - against enemy combatants, including waterboarding. But because Trump has advanced so many controversial policies - including imposing global tariffs, refusing to spend congressionally allocated funds and pushing to more broadly deploy the National Guard - the OLC now faces particular scrutiny. Critics contend that during Trump’s second term, the OLC is sometimes responding to legal questions that appear personal to Trump, rather than addressing live policy debates, as is typical. For instance, Trump had quibbled over the Presidential Records Act after he was indicted in Florida for allegedly mishandling classified materials. These critics said the OLC opinion on this act seemed aimed at Trump’s prior issues with the law, rather than any active policy issues. “It is not inconsistent with the type of advice OLC of any flavor, Democrats or Republicans, would give to other presidents,” said Carlos Uriarte, a Justice Department political appointee during the Biden administration who worked closely with the OLC. “What’s different is that this administration seems to be more willing to go into theoretical questions that are not before them.” Trump’s OLC is headed by T. Elliot Gaiser, a 37-year-old former solicitor general of Ohio described by current and former colleagues as a constitutional originalist who, like Trump, has an expansive view of executive power. Gaiser, who represented Trump’s losing presidential campaign in 2020 and refuses to acknowledge Joe Biden won that election, said his role in the Justice Department is to provide honest legal advice, not push for any particular outcome. “We’re the least interested in advocating, [and] the most interested in saying, ‘Here’s our frank view of where we think we stand in respect to the law,’” Gaiser told The Washington Post in a rare interview. His sparsely decorated office is filled with bound books of legal opinions, which surround a desk Gaiser proudly says is believed to have once been used by former Supreme Court justice Antonin Scalia, who headed the OLC under President Gerald Ford. People who know and have worked with Gaiser spoke positively about him, with former associates describing him as “brilliant.” Gaiser clerked on the Supreme Court for Samuel A. Alito Jr. when the justice wrote the landmark opinion restricting abortion access. As OLC head, Gaiser has written conservative opinions backing restrictions around abortion access, expanded gun access and greater White House authority. Gaiser said he has not hesitated to tell the White House when its ideas should not be enacted, though he declined to share specifics. Gaiser, and others familiar with the office, noted that the president is not required to listen to the OLC. Much of OLC advice is shared privately. As a result, public perceptions of the OLC are largely shaped by the opinions it releases, even as they represent only a portion of its work. The office’s role could become even more central if Democrats take control of Congress. The office recently approved an expanded view of executive privilege, for example, which Democrats fear will be used to shield Trump’s associates from testifying before Congress. Gaiser’s office could also get asked to provide legal advice if outcomes are challenged during and after next month’s midterms. The office has already determined that the executive branch can legally seek a state’s voter rolls and share them with immigration authorities - a key part of the Trump administration’s strategy to identify noncitizen voters as it tries to argue that voter fraud is rampant. Asked during the interview in his office who won the 2020 election, Gaiser demurred, citing his work as a lawyer for Trump’s campaign that year. He cannot say publicly who won, Gaiser said, because that would reveal too much about the privileged legal advice he gave Trump campaign officials when he was their attorney. “Joe Biden was sworn in as the president. He was certified the winner of the election by the Congress,” Gaiser said. “What I privately think happened in the 2020 election - what advice I provided to the president as the head of the campaign or to others in the campaign, the other campaign lawyers - that’s the kind of stuff I just really can’t get into .” Although many Trump appointees display sharp elbows and make frequent appearances on cable news shows, Gaiser takes a lower profile, even as his work is attracting increased attention, including from Democratic lawmakers and federal courts. After the OLC declared in April that the Presidential Records Act was unconstitutional, a federal court responded to lawsuits and said that, at least for now, the White House had to preserve records as normal. Advocacy groups are fighting to unseal the OLC’s memo justifying the deadly boat strikes in international waters. One former OLC attorney, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer a sensitive assessment, said the office’s opinions are based on shoddy legal arguments. Under previous administrations, “you have opinions that at least try to grapple with counterarguments,” but that is not the case today, the former OLC lawyer said. Gaiser sharply disputes the assertion that his office’s opinions are not high-quality, saying he and his lawyers deliver honest, accurate assessments. “There is a continuum with the advice you give. You can say, this is lawful but risky. This is lawfully safe. This is unlawful,” Gaiser said. “OLC has a measure of independent counsel that we offer.” During the first Trump administration, the OLC pushed back on some of the president’s most explosive actions. Steve Engel, then head of the OLC, testified about the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol that he had advised Trump appointees that some of their plans to question the results of the 2020 presidential election were not legal. Under Engel, the OLC also advised that an executive order ending birthright citizenship - the legal principal that virtually everyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen - would be unconstitutional, according to multiple people familiar with the matter, and the president did not issue one. But when Trump became president a second time, he issued an order to end birthright citizenship on his first day in office. The OLC did not review it or the other executive orders Trump issued immediately upon his return, according to two people familiar with the matter. The Supreme Court later affirmed birthright citizenship in a ruling that Trump called a “miscarriage of justice.” Gaiser, who was confirmed in July 2025, had not taken office at that point, and said his office has since reviewed all of the president’s executive orders before they are issued. The OLC attracted a burst of attention in August when it issued an opinion on executive privilege, which can shield communications between presidents and their aides. The office declared that the doctrine covers not only official advisers, but can also expand to cover outside associates consulted by the president in certain circumstances. The opinion was released as the American Bar Association was suing the Trump administration over its efforts to sanction law firms that hired Trump’s perceived foes or took on cases he disliked. The ABA is seeking testimony from Boris Epshteyn, one of Trump’s outside advisers. The ABA assailed the OLC opinion as self-serving and suspiciously timed. But Michael Edney, who worked at the OLC under Bush, said the opinion’s reading of executive privilege was not unreasonable, given the importance that some presidents place on outside consultation. “It’s not all that crazy to me,” he said. Most experts said that while OLC lawyers are not required to be blind to the president’s agenda, they cannot simply interpret the law to suit his priorities. Former OLC employees said the office should not be a rubber stamp, regardless of whether the president heeds its opinions. “In the executive branch, like everywhere else in the world, lawyers give advice and clients make decisions,” Edney said. “Their job is to provide legal advice.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/18/meet-small-doj-unit-approving-some-trumps-most-controversial-policies/

item.title: Trump approval hits record low, handing Democrats a clear midterm edge
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Two weeks from Election Day, Republicans face a bleak political landscape. President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen to a new low, and support for Democrats in the race for control of Congress is rising as inflationary pressures contribute to an acrid mood among voters, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll. Trump's approval among U.S. adults now stands at 33 percent, with 66 percent disapproving; 52 percent said they disapprove strongly. That approval rating is four percentage points lower than in July and eight points lower than at this point last year. It's lower than at any point in his first term. Among likely voters, Trump's approval is 38 percent, with 62 percent disapproving. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The poll also finds that, for the first time in more than a decade, Democrats are seen as more trusted to deal with the economy. In the competition for control of the House, Democrats hold an eight-point lead among registered and likely voters, an improvement for the party since The Post's July poll, when the Democratic lead was three points with registered voters. Trump is central to Republicans' struggles. In a separate question, the poll asked voters whether they would rather have a Democratic-led Congress acting as a check on Trump or a Republican one to support his agenda. By 58 percent to 39 percent, registered voters said they prefer the Democrats. That margin is roughly double what it was a year ago. The collective results of the new survey reveal an electorate that has lost faith in the president, is deeply worried about his decision to go to war with Iran, is feeling the effects of that war - especially the price of gasoline - on their pocketbooks and now has more confidence in Democrats than Republicans to deal with major issues. Today, 72 percent say the country is heading in the wrong direction, up five points since April. The new survey findings do not predict how individual House or Senate races will turn out in November. But they help to explain why Republicans are on the defensive in these final weeks, even in areas where they have traditionally held a strong advantage. Republicans still enjoy an overall lead in money to pour into political advertising that they hope will hold back the Democratic tide. Tellingly, those resources are shifting to protect some candidates in redder areas, a sign of the growing concerns among party leaders and strategists about the overall climate. As always, the question of who turns out to vote will decide how individual races go, with many of the most competitive Senate races still in the balance. Nationally, Democrats have a big advantage among those who said they're "certain to vote" or have already done so, but Republicans fare relatively well among voters who turned out in the 2024 or 2022 elections, which are also strong predictors of voting. One critical unknown is how many of Trump's 77 million voters from the 2024 election will cast ballots. Midterm turnout is always lower than in presidential years and Republicans have had a harder time turning out their supporters when Trump is not on the ballot. The poll echoes those challenges. Democratic registered voters are more likely than Republicans to say they are certain to vote or have already done so, 75 percent versus 67 percent. While 75 percent of Republicans who support the MAGA movement say they're certain to vote, that drops to 57 percent among non-MAGA Republicans (though more than a quarter of these non-MAGA Republicans said they prefer Democrats in control of the next Congress). By contrast, 79 percent of Democrats who support the Democratic Socialists of America say they are certain to vote, as do 73 percent of nonsocialist Democrats. Presidential approval has long been one of the most important indicators of how a midterm election will go. Based on history, Republicans are poised to lose seats from their narrow House majority and likely to lose control of the chamber next month. But how many is more difficult to predict because, in contrast to some past years, there are fewer swing districts. Republicans may also retain backing from voters who expressed only limited dissatisfaction with the president. The Post-ABC-Ipsos poll finds that among the 10 percent of likely voters who said they "somewhat disapprove" of Trump's performance, 58 percent prefer the Republican candidate for the House. Economic issues stand as a major threat to the GOP's hold on the House and Senate. Trump's economic approval rating has fallen to 28 percent, down from 33 percent in July, 41 percent in February and 49 percent at this point in the 2018 midterm election campaign. About 3 in 4 Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of inflation and the cost of living in the United States. By a 3-1 margin, Americans said the state of the economy is either not so good or poor. Most Republicans (53 percent) rate the economy positively compared with 9 percent of Democrats and 16 percent of independents. At this point in 2022, when President Joe Biden was in office, impressions of the economy were almost identically negative. But in a sign of how party allegiance can affect attitudes, 54 percent of Democrats then rated the economy positively, compared with 8 percent of Republicans and 16 percent of independents. Economic strains on many Americans are great enough that 48 percent say they are financially worse off than when Trump returned to office in 2025. That represents the highest percentage saying this about any president in Post-ABC polls since 1986. Among these financially stressed Americans, 78 percent favor Democrats for Congress, along with 71 percent of independents. Affordability is an issue that nearly all candidates are talking about this fall and the survey points to many areas of difficulty for families. The biggest is the cost of gasoline. In February, before Trump launched the war with Iran, 71 percent said gasoline was affordable. Today, as the war has disrupted supplies and shipping, pushing up gasoline and diesel prices significantly, perceptions have flipped, with 71 percent now saying gasoline is not affordable. Majorities also say groceries, health care and home energy are unaffordable, all up significantly since before the Iran war. Fewer than 4 in 10 said going out to dinner is affordable, down from half who said this in February. The shift against the president ripples throughout the survey. On Iran, 65 percent said it was a mistake to take military action and 68 percent disapprove of the way Trump has dealt with U.S. allies. Roughly 6 in 10 disapprove of his handling of immigration, a sharp departure from the beginning of his second term when 50 percent said they approved. A majority (56 percent) said Trump has gone too far in deporting undocumented immigrants, which compares with 48 percent in April 2025 as the deportation effort was beginning. Trump's negative ratings are boosted by significant criticism from his 2024 voters, including 23 percent who disapprove of his overall performance, 31 percent who disapprove of his management of the economy and 38 percent who disapprove of his handling of inflation. Most of these critics said they support Republicans for Congress, but they're far less certain about casting ballots this year than Trump voters who approve of him. Trump is judged harshly on several measures of his commitment to fundamental principles of democracy. At least 6 in 10 people said he is not committed to protecting freedom of the press and freedom of speech, free and fair elections, and respecting the authority of Congress or the courts. Beyond major issues, the public disapproves of the ways Trump has conducted himself in office. The poll finds that 66 percent said he is using the presidency to enrich himself, up from 56 percent last fall. Eight in 10 think it is inappropriate that he has pushed to put his name on the Kennedy Center in Washington (59 percent view this as "completely inappropriate"), and 74 percent say it's inappropriate that the federal government paid for television ads promoting Trump and his policies. Overall, 66 percent said they see Trump as "too extreme." The dissatisfaction with Trump inevitably has spilled onto a Republican Party that has been remade in his image. Registered voters said they trust Democrats over Republicans to handle the economy by 40 percent to 33 percent, the first Democratic advantage on the economy in Post-ABC polling since 2014. Voters split about evenly on this question in April and July of this year. Democrats also hold double-digit advantages on trust to handle inflation and the cost of living. Democrats are seen as more trustworthy on many issues even though 54 percent of U.S. adults have an unfavorable view of the party, perhaps because even more Americans - 63 percent - dislike the Republican Party. The Republican Party is seen as too extreme by 55 percent of U.S. adults, compared with 36 percent who see the Democratic Party that way. Americans hold negative impressions of the president's MAGA movement and of democratic socialism, which has roiled the Democratic Party this year. But the MAGA movement is seen even more negatively at 69 percent unfavorable compared with 59 percent unfavorable toward democratic socialism. One-quarter of Americans dislike both major political parties, but as often happens, these "double-haters" swing against the party in power, favoring Democrats by 58 percent to 32 percent in support for Congress. One factor boosting Democrats this fall, and another sign of how Trump's policies and performance have hurt him and his party, is a shift in the partisan leanings of Americans. The Pew Research Center's annual benchmarking survey - a comprehensive poll conducted over several months - found 47 percent of U.S. adults identified as Democrats or lean Democratic this spring, while 43 percent identified as or leaned Republican. That marked a shift from both 2025, when 46 percent of adults identified as Republicans and 45 percent as Democrats. Post-ABC-Ipsos polls are calibrated to match Pew's estimates for partisanship, and the latest poll reflects the national shift in party leanings. Read detailed results and cross tabs from the Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll . The poll was conducted online Oct. 9-13 among 2,545 U.S. adults nationwide reached through the Ipsos KnowledgePanel, an ongoing panel of U.S. households recruited by mail using random sampling methods. Overall results have a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points. The error margin is plus or minus 2.2 points for results among 2,032 registered voters and likely voters; all registered voters were assigned a probability of voting to produce likely voter results. The sample was weighted to match population demographics, 2024 turnout/vote choice and political partisanship. - - - Graphics: President Trump's approval rating reaches record low Democrats hold eight-point advantage in national support for Congress Democratic-leaning groups more certain about voting in 2026 midterms Economic ratings similar to before 2022 midterms, far worse than in 2018 Record high say they are 'not as well off' financially as when Trump entered office More Americans see gas, staples and splurges are "unaffordable" Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-approval-hits-record-low-140856093.html

item.title: A timeline of the Cornell rape case, from the alleged 2024 incident to the frat party ban
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The investigation into an alleged "gang rape" at Cornell University in October 2024 has drawn nationwide attention after a former student identified as "Jane Doe" filed a civil lawsuit last month, accusing seven fraternity members of drugging and assaulting her for hours. Last week, Cornell announced that it is suspending "all parties and social events" at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year while an independent review is underway. "These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue," Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the Cornell community . Kotlikoff also announced that the university would enlist "experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators" to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its Ithaca, N.Y., campus. Earlier this month, Cornell's board of trustees announced it had retained former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, a partner at law firm King & Spalding, to lead an outside review of how the university responds to sexual assault. Separately, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation after losing faith in both Cornell and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who initially declined to bring charges in the Jane Doe case. "This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable," the governor said. "And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her." All of the men identified in Jane Doe's civil suit have denied any wrongdoing, according to the New York Times . None has been charged with a crime. On Friday, a New York judge denied a request from one of the accused fraternity members for a gag order in Jane Doe’s civil case. Here is a timeline of the case, from the alleged incident to the reopening of a criminal investigation, culled from Jane Doe's civil lawsuit, statements from Cornell and public officials, and other reports. August 2022 "Jane Doe" begins her freshman year at Cornell University, where she joins a sorority, Tri-Delta's Alpha Beta Chapter. Oct. 19-20, 2024 Jane Doe drinks vodka at her residence at the sorority before attending a Tri-Delta event hosted at Moonies Bar and Nightclub, where she is allegedly served alcohol despite identifying herself as underage. Around 11 p.m., Jane Doe walks to the Chi Phi fraternity house, arriving "visibly intoxicated" after consuming "about 10 standard drinks within the past 3 hours," according to her civil lawsuit. Shortly after arriving, Jane Doe is allegedly pressured by two fraternity brothers into snorting what they said was ketamine before taking part in a threesome proposed by the men. "In her drunken state, Plaintiff was incapable of consenting to this proposition," the lawsuit alleges. At 1:41 a.m., one of the men sends a message to the fraternity's Snapchat group suggesting that she was available for sex, according to the lawsuit, which included a screengrab of part of the group chat. The complaint alleges that multiple fraternity members show up and rape her over several hours. During the alleged assault, the fraternity members begin "pouring lines of Ketamine all over her body and snorting them," per the complaint. At around 5:45 a.m., the alleged assault ends and Jane Doe loses consciousness, her lawsuit states. Later that day, Jane Doe returns to the sorority house "in a state of shock," per her suit. Oct. 21, 2024 Jane Doe exchanges text messages with one of the men she would later name in the lawsuit, who tells her, "I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night," according to the New York Times . She replies: "At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt." Oct. 22, 2024 Jane Doe makes an appointment at Cornell Health for a urinary tract infection and wants to be tested for sexually transmitted diseases, telling the doctor she contracted it "in a traumatic way," per the Times. The doctor doesn't follow up and suggests she "go to therapy." Oct. 23, 2024 In another text exchange, Jane Doe tells one of the fraternity members that "my reputation is destroyed and I'm utterly ashamed," according to ABC News . In the same exchange, she also says: "everyone needs to grow up because sexuality and sex and [stuff] is changing and stuff like this is going to become more common. i'm also really open minded tho. i love u king." Oct. 30, 2024 Jane Doe sends a text to the same frat member saying she was "uninvited" to an upcoming Chi Phi Halloween party. "i knew this was going to happen. the woman will always get the short end of the stick," she writes. "yall aren't my friends. yall are covering your a****." Nov. 7, 2024 In a recorded phone call with one of the fraternity members, Jane Doe says she was "10 shots deep" when she arrived at the Chi Phi fraternity house and is now struggling to remember what happened, according to audio obtained by ABC News. The fraternity member insists Jane Doe told him she was sober before the alleged encounter, which she denies. At one point during the call, Jane Doe tells him, "If I wanted to take this somewhere, what y'all did would be classified as gang rape." The fraternity member then suggests that their memory of what transpired may be inaccurate. Jane Doe pushes back: "No, because I remember looking up and being like, 'That is too many people.'" Nov. 8, 2024 Jane Doe reports the Oct. 19-20 incident to campus police. Nov. 14, 2024 According to CBS News , Jane Doe gives an interview to campus police in which she states: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped." (Van Houten later says his office was not provided with a transcript of that interview when it decided not to pursue charges.) Nov. 15, 2024 Jane Doe gives a sworn statement to campus police in which she says that the incident "felt like coercion," according to ABC News . She recalls that at one point, she said "no to the foursome" that one of the fraternity brothers had proposed. She also states: "I remember being totally disgusted at the situation, and I felt very tired and intoxicated. I would say that my level of overall intoxication was about a 8 out of 10 level of intoxicated. I would say that it was the most intoxicated I've ever been in my life. I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was." Nov. 26, 2024 Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff publishes an open letter to students and alumni with an update on the "ongoing investigations into the serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house." He says that "interim measures in the form of temporary suspensions were issued for a number of students to protect the immediate physical health and safety of all students." "The behavior that has been outlined in the many allegations received is abhorrent and cannot be tolerated within our community. I urge anyone who has experienced or is aware of sexual misconduct on our campus to report it," he adds. "Only those who perpetrate sexual violence benefit from its concealment." Jan. 14, 2025 Cornell commences a Title IX investigation in response to Jane Doe's allegations, according to her lawsuit, holding at least 12 hearings over a four-week period in May. According to ABC News , Jane Doe tells the school's investigators that she "felt like bait" on the night of the alleged assault. "I felt like lions around me," she says during one of the hearings. The comments are included in a 99-page report prepared in August by the university as part of its Title IX investigation, per ABC. The report also includes comments from a fraternity member who Cornell's investigation later concluded did not engage in the assault but was found responsible for "attempted sexual exploitation." "I was sorry that maybe if it wasn't consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it," the fraternity member says, according to ABC. According to the New York Times , Jane Doe tells Cornell's Title IX investigators that she did not consider herself a victim until she saw the incident being discussed as a "gang rape" in an online forum. "That's the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn't a whore and that I was assaulted," Jane Doe tells investigators, per the Times. Feb. 6, 2025 Cornell establishes a Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault that is "charged with understanding and addressing sexual assault involving undergraduate students on the Ithaca campus." March 10, 2026 Cornell University releases the task force's final report with recommendations aimed at "developing a holistic public health framework for addressing sexual assault": "By improving communication, education, transparency, and access to resources, we can ensure students are well-informed and supported as we work to confront sexual assault at Cornell," the school says . "Among the key measures in the report are launching a public health campaign; increasing students' knowledge and clarity of reporting options and confidential resources; developing new educational opportunities, including courses focused on sexual citizenship; prioritizing evidence‑based prevention strategies; and expanding training for students, leaders, and residential staff." Sept. 16, 2026 Jane Doe files a civil lawsuit in New York State Supreme Court against Cornell University, seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, the Chi Phi and Tri-Delta Alpha Beta House chapters and the owners of Moonies Bar & Nightclub. Sept. 21, 2026 Cornell University releases a statement saying it is aware of "a lawsuit concerning the deeply disturbing allegations of sexual assault involving members of the student community that occurred in 2024." The university says that it "adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies," adding: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students and we therefore are unable to make a public statement on any other disciplinary response." Sept. 28, 2026 Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, announces that he has reopened a criminal investigation into the alleged incident. Van Houten describes the allegations as "morally disturbing," but argues that the facts he knew at the time did not support a prosecution. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later," Van Houten says in a lengthy statement that sought to explain why he initially decided not to prosecute the case. Cornell releases a statement saying it supports the district attorney's decision to reopen the case, while pushing back against critics who say it did not "impose consequential punishments for those involved." "The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence," the school says. "At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement." Oct. 1, 2026 Hochul says she has lost faith in Van Houten and signs an executive order appointing New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the investigation. Oct. 2, 2026 Hochul holds a press conference with James to explain her appointment as special prosecutor, saying Jane Doe was "failed" by people obligated to protect her. "In what world would the police learn from a victim that she'd been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?" Hochul says. "In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved or even request the full transcript?" James says that the case is "now an active criminal investigation." "We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions," she says, adding: "I know that you want answers. I do too." Oct. 3, 2026 Kotlikoff, Cornell's president, posts an eight-minute video statement , saying it "has been one of the most difficult weeks" in the university's history, and that the school "must do better" to address sexual assault and substance abuse on campus. "What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff says. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use. It also raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported." Oct. 4, 2026 Jane Doe's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, says his client has received "multiple threats" in recent days from people who want her to withdraw her lawsuit. item.title: 'It's like a war zone': Fresh clashes break out in Paris after historic day of unrest
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Sybille de La Hamaide, Clotaire Achi and Abdul Saboor PARIS/LIMOGES, Oct 18 (Reuters) - President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday, a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with thousands arrested and shops looted or damaged after protests over high prices and declining public services. Fresh ‌clashes broke out in Paris and Marseille, where riot police intervened to prevent attempts to ransack businesses. Nationwide demonstrations had erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town ‌hall torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country. "Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do ​this to France?" Macron said in a televised address to the nation. "Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame." Saturday's unrest laid bare the deep anger at Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt. Macron said those protesting peacefully had legitimate grievances and their actions should not be confused with those seeking to wreak havoc. He stopped short of declaring a state of emergency, as demanded by some right-wing politicians, but said the government would act to ‌allow prefects to ban protests if necessary to protect public buildings ⁠and local businesses. PARIS PROTESTS 'LIKE A WAR ZONE' The government has blamed the violence on what it said were ultra-left groups, as well as criminals it said had instigated the looting. One protester died on Saturday after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris. Police made 2,400 arrests across France, ⁠while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. Police again clashed with protesters and fired tear gas at Place de la Republique on Sunday afternoon, and protesters had set fire to piles of bicycles. A Reuters witness said there appeared to be several hundred protesters in the area. A massive clean-up operation took place in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and ​from ​Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the ​local prefect. "It's like a war zone here!" exclaimed Dutch entrepreneur Tije De ‌Boer, who was visiting Paris with his children and said the unrest forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique. More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities on Saturday, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services. SEVERAL HUNDRED SHOPS DAMAGED While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully across France on Saturday, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers. Far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, frontrunner going into next year's presidential campaign, also called for calm, saying France must not become accustomed to images of the country being battered, abused and ransacked. "Violence is not an opinion. Destruction is not a ‌form of expression. And chaos cannot serve as a project for France," she said in a video address. Hard-left ​France Unbowed presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Macron needed to answer the demands of protesting high-school students. In Limoges, ​famed for its porcelain, the collapse of the town hall's clock tower in a ​fiery blaze revived memories of the 2019 fire that devastated Paris' Notre Dame cathedral. Mayor Guillaume Guerin said not enough officers from the national police ‌had been deployed to his city. "There was a clear, premeditated intention to ​burn down the town hall, and the people ​inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters on Sunday. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the funds needed to repair the town hall. Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to ​sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement. French retailer Carrefour's CEO Alexandre ‌Bompard told French broadcaster BFMTV that 50 of the company's shops had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into ​the tens of millions of euros. (Reporting by Sybille de La Hamaide, Janis Laizans, Abdul Saboor, Clotaire Achi, Marc Leras, Michel Rose, Elizabeth Pineau, Natasa Bansagi; Writing ​by Sybille de la Hamaide; Editing by Richard Lough, Elaine Hardcastle, Jan Harvey and Edmund Klamann) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/france-faces-aftermath-worst-unrest-094920368.html

In a caption of an Instagram post, the group's page said: “We’re proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday.” The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Maine, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had “zero coordination” with Jackson's campaign.
